title: Refund
outcomes: Apply the refund procedure and time limits under section 27.
Apply the doctrine of unjust enrichment.
Apply refund of export and import duty in special cases.

meta.exam_tip: Check limitation first, then unjust enrichment, then interest.

concepts.title: Claiming refund under section 27
body: Section 27: a person who paid or bore duty or interest may apply for refund within one year from the date of payment; a buyer who bore the duty counts from the date of purchase. Where duty was paid under protest, no limitation applies. No refund is paid where the amount is below ₹100.

The one-year period runs from special dates in some cases: from the date of the appellate order or judgment where refund follows it, from adjustment of duty after final assessment where duty was provisionally paid, and from payment of duty on a revised entry under section 149 or 46.
The application must be accompanied by documents showing the duty was paid and the incidence was not passed on. Section 27 is a complete code; refund outside it cannot be sought through civil suits.
concepts.analogy: One year, unless paid under protest.
concepts.work: Excess duty paid due to a wrong rate can be claimed within twelve months.

concepts.title: Unjust enrichment and the Consumer Welfare Fund
body: Unjust enrichment: a refund should go only to the person who actually bore the duty. Section 28D presumes that every person who paid duty has passed on its incidence to the buyer, unless proved otherwise.

If the applicant cannot rebut the presumption, the refundable amount is credited to the Consumer Welfare Fund. It is paid to the applicant where: the importer or exporter had not passed it on; an individual imported for personal use; the buyer bore it without passing it on; it relates to export duty refunded under section 26; it relates to drawback under sections 74 and 75; it was borne by a notified class; or excess duty was paid before the home-clearance order and is evident from the self-assessed or reassessed bill of entry.

The Supreme Court upheld the doctrine as valid (Mafatlal Industries) and held it applies even to duty paid under protest; an unchanged selling price alone does not prove that the burden was absorbed (Allied Photographics).
concepts.analogy: No windfall: refund follows the burden.
concepts.work: An importer who priced duty into its sales gets no refund; the money goes to the Fund.

concepts.title: Interest on delayed refund
body: Section 27A: if refund is not paid within 3 months of receipt of a complete application, interest is payable from the day after those 3 months till the refund date. The rate may be fixed between 5% and 30%; currently 6% per annum.
Where refund arises from an order of the Commissioner (Appeals), Tribunal or court, that order is treated as the refund order and the 3-month clock runs from it.

Excess duty found on final assessment of a provisional assessment must be refunded within 3 months; otherwise interest at the section 27A rate is payable under section 18(4). Deposits like project-import security carry no interest.
concepts.analogy: Three months to pay, then six percent.
concepts.work: Refund paid five months after application earns about two months' interest.

concepts.title: Refund of export and import duty in special cases
body: Section 26: export duty is refunded where goods are returned to the exporter otherwise than by resale, re-imported within one year of export, and the claim is made within 6 months of the clearance order on re-import.

Section 26A: import duty is refunded where goods are defective or not to specification, not worked on or used (except to discover the defect), identifiable, no drawback is claimed, and the goods are exported, abandoned to customs, or destroyed or rendered commercially valueless within 30 days of the clearance order (extendable by up to 3 months).

The 26A claim is due within 6 months of the relevant date (e.g. the export order or relinquishment). It is unavailable for perishables, goods whose shelf life expired, notified goods, or goods involved in an offence.
concepts.analogy: Special refunds for returned exports and rejected imports.
concepts.work: A defective imported analyser re-exported within 30 days earns a refund of import duty.

model.title: Section 27(1)

summary: Section 27: one year; none if under protest; minimum ₹100.
Section 26: export duty, re-import within one year, claim in 6 months.
Section 26A: defective imports, 30 days + 3 months, claim in 6 months.
remember: Section 18(4): interest on refund after final assessment.
traps: Counting interest from sanction instead of application date.

viva.q: Who may claim refund besides the importer?
viva.model: A buyer who bore the duty, within one year from the date of purchase.

viva.q: When is refund of excess duty paid to the importer despite the presumption?
viva.model: When excess payment before the clearance order is evident from the bill of entry.

viva.q: From when does interest run on a refund ordered in appeal?
viva.model: Three months after the appellate order, which is treated as the refund order.

viva.q: Can goods used after import get section 26A refund?
viva.model: Only where use was indispensable to discover the defect.

viva.q: Is interest payable on security deposits?
viva.model: Section 27A covers delayed refunds of duty only, so deposits like provisional-release security carry no interest.

cases.case: Yamuna Minerals paid export duty on ore shipped in May of year 1. The buyer rejected it, and the ore was re-imported in March of year 2 (cleared 10 March).
